question: My mom just turned 65 and is signing up for Medicare. How much will her Part B premium be each month in 2026, and is there anything that could make it higher?
expected_answer: The standard Part B premium in 2026 is $202.90 a month, and most people pay that standard amount. She would pay more only if she owes an Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount (IRMAA), which applies when the modified adjusted gross income on the tax return from 2 years ago was above the limit: for 2026, a 2024 income above $109,000 filing individually or $218,000 married filing jointly. The handbook points to Medicare.gov for IRMAA details and to SSA.gov/medicare/lower-irmaa to disagree with the extra charge.

evidence.quote: The standard Part B premium amount in 2026 is $202.90. Most people pay the standard Part B premium amount every month.
For 2026, if your modified adjusted gross income for 2024 was above $109,000 if you file individually or $218,000 if you’re married and file jointly, then you may pay an IRMAA.

question: Dad has Original Medicare and no other insurance. He spent 5 days in the hospital and then went straight into a skilled nursing facility for 30 days. What will he owe for that in 2026?
expected_answer: About $3,906 in Part A charges. He pays the $1,736 Part A deductible once for the benefit period, and hospital days 1–60 cost $0 a day after it, so the 5 hospital days add nothing more. He does not pay the deductible a second time at the skilled nursing facility because he already paid it in the same benefit period; SNF days 1–20 are $0 a day and days 21–100 are $217 a day, so the 10 days over 20 cost 10 × $217 = $2,170. A correct answer must give the $1,736 deductible, the $217 daily SNF rate, and the fact that the deductible is not charged twice in one benefit period.

evidence.quote: Each time you start a new benefit period, you must pay $1,736 (in 2026) before Medicare starts to pay.
Days 1–60: After you pay the $1,736 Part A deductible, you pay $0 each day.
Days 1–20: You pay $0 each day after you pay the $1,736 amount.
Days 21–100: You pay $217 each day.
you don’t have to pay the Part A deductible for skilled nursing facility care if you already paid it for care you got in a hospital during the same benefit period

question: What are the 2026 income and resource limits for qualifying for Extra Help with Medicare drug costs?
expected_answer: The handbook does not give the 2026 limits. The only limits it prints are the 2025 ones (single person: yearly income less than $23,475 and resources less than $17,600; married person living with a spouse and no other dependents: less than $31,725 and less than $35,130), and it says the 2026 income and resource limits can be found on Medicare.gov. A correct answer says the 2026 figures are not in the handbook and points to Medicare.gov, and may add SSA.gov/extrahelp to apply or 1-800-MEDICARE.

evidence.quote: You may qualify for Extra Help if your yearly income and resources are below these limits in 2025:
You can find 2026 income and resource limits on Medicare.gov.

question: My mother is having trouble hearing. Does Original Medicare pay for hearing aids, or for the exam to fit them?
expected_answer: No to both. Original Medicare does not cover hearing aids or the exams for fitting them, so she would have to pay for those herself. What it does cover is a diagnostic hearing and balance (fall risk) exam that her doctor or other health care provider orders to see if she needs medical treatment, and one audiologist visit every 12 months without an order for non-acute hearing conditions; for those she pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount and the Part B deductible applies.

evidence.quote: Note: Original Medicare doesn’t cover hearing aids or exams for fitting hearing aids.
Medicare covers diagnostic hearing and balance (fall risk) exams if your doctor or health care provider orders them to see if you need medical treatment.
You can visit an audiologist once every 12 months without an order from a doctor or other health care provider, but only for non-acute hearing conditions
You pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount. The Part B deductible applies.
Hearing aids and exams for fitting them.

question: I'm 68 and still working at a company with 12 employees, and I have the company health plan as well as Medicare. Which one pays my medical bills first?
expected_answer: Medicare pays first. The handbook's coordination chart says that if you are 65 or older and have group health plan coverage based on your or your spouse's current employment and the employer has fewer than 20 employees, Medicare pays first. The group health plan would pay first only if the employer had 20 or more employees, or had fewer than 20 but was part of a multi-employer plan that includes other employers with 20 or more employees.

evidence.quote: If you’re 65 or older, have group health plan coverage based on your or your spouse’s current employment, and the employer has fewer than 20 employees... Medicare pays first.
the employer has 20 or more employees OR your employer has fewer than 20 employees but is part of a multi-employer plan

question: My mom turns 65 on March 12. When can she sign up for Medicare without paying a penalty, and when would her coverage start?
expected_answer: Her Initial Enrollment Period for Part A and Part B is the 7-month window that begins 3 months before the month she turns 65 and ends 3 months after it, so December through June. (The shifted window only applies if the birthday falls on the first of the month, and hers does not.) If she signs up during the first 3 months, December through February, coverage generally begins on March 1, the first day of her birthday month. If she signs up in March itself or in April, May or June, coverage starts the first day of the month after she signs up.

evidence.quote: Generally, you can first sign up for Part A and/or Part B during the 7-month period that begins 3 months before the month you turn 65 and ends 3 months after the month you turn 65.
in most cases, your coverage begins the first day of your birthday month
If you sign up the month you turn 65 or during the last 3 months of your Initial Enrollment Period, your coverage starts the first day of the month after you sign up.

question: My husband is retiring in April and I'm 67 and covered by his employer's health plan. How long will I have to sign up for Part B, and does taking COBRA buy me more time?
expected_answer: You can sign up any time you are still covered by the group health plan, and then during the 8-month Special Enrollment Period that begins the month after the employment ends or the coverage ends, whichever happens first. Signing up in that window usually means no late enrollment penalty. COBRA does not extend it: COBRA is not coverage based on current employment, so the 8 months run from the end of the employment-based coverage whether or not you take COBRA, and you generally will not get another Special Enrollment Period when the COBRA ends.

evidence.quote: During the 8-month period that begins the month after the employment ends or the coverage ends, whichever happens first
Usually, you won’t have to pay a late enrollment penalty if you sign up during a Special Enrollment Period.
After coverage based on current employment ends, you have 8 months to sign up for Part B without a penalty, whether or not you choose COBRA.
You generally aren’t eligible for a Special Enrollment Period to sign up for Medicare when that COBRA coverage ends.

question: I turn 65 on August 14, I'm still working, and I put money into a health savings account through my job. If I sign up for Medicare during my Initial Enrollment Period, when does my last HSA contribution have to be?
expected_answer: July, the month before you turn 65. The handbook's chart says that if you sign up for Medicare during your Initial Enrollment Period you can avoid a tax penalty by making your last HSA contribution the month before you turn 65. The reason is that you cannot contribute to an HSA once you have Medicare, and the handbook says to make your last contribution the month before your Part A coverage begins. Premium-free Part A goes back (retroactively) 6 months from when you sign up for Part A or apply for Social Security or RRB benefits, but no earlier than the first month you are eligible for Medicare, so that 6-month lookback is what moves the cut-off earlier in the chart's other rows, not in yours.

evidence.quote: You aren’t eligible to make contributions to an HSA after you have Medicare.
Consider making your last HSA contribution the month before your Part A coverage begins
You can avoid a tax penalty by making your last HSA contribution the month before you turn 65
Premium-free Part A coverage will go back (retroactively) 6 months from when you sign up for Part A or apply for benefits

question: Mom has Original Medicare and nothing else. Is there a cap on what she can be charged out of pocket in a year, and would a Medicare Advantage plan cap it?
expected_answer: Under Original Medicare there is no yearly limit on what she pays out of pocket unless she has supplemental coverage such as Medigap, Medicaid, or employer, retiree or union coverage. Medicare Advantage Plans do have a yearly limit on what you pay for covered Medicare services, which may include different limits for in-network and out-of-network services, and once she reached her plan's limit she would pay nothing for covered services for the rest of the year. The handbook gives no dollar amount for that limit.

evidence.quote: There’s no yearly limit on what you pay out of pocket, unless you have supplemental coverage—like Medicare Supplement Insurance (Medigap), Medicaid, employer, retiree, or union coverage.
Plans have a yearly limit on what you pay for covered Medicare services (which may include different limits for in-network and out-of-network services).
Once you reach your plan’s limit, you’ll pay nothing for covered services for the rest of the year.

question: My mother found a Medicare Advantage plan with a $0 monthly premium. Does that mean she would pay nothing each month for her Medicare?
expected_answer: No. A $0 plan premium does not remove the Part B premium: she still pays that every month, plus a Part A premium if she does not have premium-free Part A. If a plan does charge its own premium, she pays that on top of the Part B premium. Some Medicare Advantage Plans will help pay all or part of the Part B premium, sometimes called a "Medicare Part B premium reduction," so she should check whether that particular plan does.

evidence.quote: Some Medicare Advantage Plans have a $0 premium (but you still may pay the Part B premium).
If you join a plan that charges a premium, you pay this in addition to the Part B premium (and the Part A premium if you don’t have premium-free Part A).
Some Medicare Advantage Plans will help pay all or part of your Part B premium. This is sometimes called a “Medicare Part B premium reduction.”
You pay the monthly Part B premium and may also have to pay the plan’s premium. Some plans may have a $0 premium and may help pay all or part of your Part B premium.

question: My father takes several expensive prescriptions. Is there any cap on what he'll have to pay for his drugs in 2026?
expected_answer: Yes, if he has Medicare drug coverage (Part D). Yearly out-of-pocket costs for drugs covered by his plan are capped at $2,100 in 2026. Once he reaches that cap, counting his own out-of-pocket spending plus certain payments other people or entities make, including Medicare's Extra Help program, he pays no copayment or coinsurance for covered Part D drugs for the rest of the calendar year. The cap only covers drugs his plan covers.

evidence.quote: Your yearly out-of-pocket drug costs for drugs covered by your plan are capped at $2,100 in 2026.
you won’t have to pay a copayment or coinsurance for covered Part D drugs for the rest of the calendar year.

your yearly out-of-pocket Part D drugs are capped at $2,100 in 2026. Once you reach this cap, you won’t have to pay a copayment or coinsurance for covered Part D drugs for the rest of the calendar year

question: Does Medicare drug coverage pay for Eliquis? My mom wants to know before she picks a plan.
expected_answer: The handbook does not say. It states that information about a plan's list of covered drugs, called a formulary, is not included in the handbook because each plan has its own formulary, and that you should review a plan's formulary before joining. A correct answer says the handbook does not list covered drugs and points her to the plan itself or to Medicare.gov/plan-compare, and may add 1-800-MEDICARE or her State Health Insurance Assistance Program. It may also note that all plans must cover a wide range of drugs, including most drugs in certain protected classes.

evidence.quote: Information about a plan’s list of covered drugs (called a “formulary”) isn’t included in this handbook because each plan has its own formulary.
Visit Medicare.gov/plan-compare to find and compare plans in your area.

question: Dad is 68, has had Medicare since he was 65 and never joined a drug plan because he takes no medication. If he joins one now, will he be charged a penalty, and how is it worked out?
expected_answer: Yes, unless he had other creditable prescription drug coverage or gets Extra Help. The late enrollment penalty applies when you enroll after your Initial Enrollment Period is over and there was a period of 63 or more days in a row without Medicare drug coverage or other creditable prescription drug coverage, and it is permanently added to the Part D premium for as long as you have Medicare drug coverage. The amount is 1% of the national base beneficiary premium ($38.99 in 2026) multiplied by the number of full, uncovered months, rounded to the nearest $0.10.

evidence.quote: there’s a period of 63 or more days in a row when you don’t have Medicare drug coverage or other creditable prescription drug coverage
If you get Extra Help, you don’t pay a late enrollment penalty.
calculated by multiplying 1% of the “national base beneficiary premium” ($38.99 in 2026) by the number of full, uncovered months
The final amount is rounded to the nearest $.10 and added to your monthly premium.
you don’t have other creditable prescription drug coverage (like drug coverage from an employer or union) or get Extra Help, you’ll likely pay a late enrollment penalty
Generally, you’ll pay this penalty for as long as you have Medicare drug coverage

question: Dad is comparing Medigap Plan K and Plan L. What is the most each one would let him pay out of pocket in 2026, and how much of his costs do they cover?
expected_answer: In 2026 Plan K's yearly out-of-pocket limit is $8,000 and Plan L's is $4,000. After he meets that limit and the yearly Part B deductible ($283 in 2026), the Medigap plan pays 100% of covered services for the rest of the calendar year. Until then, Plan K pays 50% and Plan L pays 75% of the Part B coinsurance or copayment, the blood benefit for the first 3 pints, the Part A hospice care coinsurance or copayment, skilled nursing facility care coinsurance, and the Part A deductible; both pay 100% of the Part A coinsurance and hospital costs, and neither covers the Part B deductible, Part B excess charges, or foreign travel emergency care.

evidence.quote: Out-of-pocket limit in 2026** $8,000 $4,000
For Plans K and L, after you meet your out-of-pocket yearly limit and your yearly Part B deductible ($283 in 2026), the Medigap plan pays 100% of covered services for the rest of the calendar year.
Medicare Part B coinsurance or copayment 100% 100% 100% 100% 100% 100% 50% 75% 100% 100%***

question: When is the best time for my dad to buy a Medigap policy, and what happens if he waits?
expected_answer: The best time is his Medigap Open Enrollment Period, the 6-month period that begins the first month he has Medicare Part B and is 65 or older. After that period he may not be able to buy a Medigap policy at all, or it may cost more, although in certain situations he may have guaranteed issue rights outside it and some states have additional open enrollment periods. He must generally have both Part A and Part B before he can buy Medigap, and if he delays Part B because of group health coverage based on current employment, his Medigap Open Enrollment Period does not start until he gets Part B.

evidence.quote: This 6-month period begins the first month you have Medicare Part B (Medical Insurance), and you’re 65 or older.
After this enrollment period, you may not be able to buy a Medigap policy or it may cost more.
Before you can buy Medicare Supplement Insurance (Medigap), you must generally have Part A and Part B.
